references.text: Rebekah serves as the active intermediary who transfers her father's words from the planning phase to the crisis phase.
An ironic contrast between Rebekah's ability to 'hear' the truth of her father's words and Isaac's failed attempt to recognize his son based on voice.
A direct narrative connection where Rebekah's recounting of her father's words (v. 6) leads directly to Jacob's execution of those words (v. 19).
A thematic parallel concerning the 'voice' as a sign of identity: in v. 6, the voice is a source of information; in v. 22, it becomes a source of doubt and confusion.
A causal link: Rebekah hearing words about Esau (v. 6) leads directly to the situation where Isaac must ask 'Who are you?' when the false Esau is exposed (v. 32).
A thematic contrast showing the development in the brothers' relationship: from Rebekah's fear of Esau's revenge (v. 6) to Jacob's attempt to calm Esau's anger (Gen 32:5).
A narrative parallel concerning 'hearing a decree of fate': Rebekah hears her father's plan (v. 6), which triggers the event; Esau hears the outcome (v. 34), which concludes it.
